video.title: Deeper Than Just "Footwork" | Tennis Movement Fundamentals Explained

classification.reason: The coach analyzes Roger Federer's glide steps and single-foot balance mechanics, explains root causes behind poor stance and balance, and presents progressive physical movement drills.

problem.title_as_question: Why do players struggle to move explosively and glide smoothly on court like Federer?
problem.definition: Players move with a narrow, upright base, land flatfooted after the split step, and lack the single-leg balance and physical capacity to absorb forces dynamically without flailing their upper body.
prerequisites: Basic tracking of the ball over the net
problem.target_player: Tennis players who struggle to get wide, land flatfooted, or feel narrow and unbalanced during movement

symptoms.description: The player lands flatfooted after the split step rather than moving continuously into the shot.
The player's feet stay narrow and together with weight resting back on the heels during recovery and preparation.
The player feels unable to push laterally or explosively to either side, feeling restricted to pushing mostly up and down.

causes.statement: The stance is too narrow, preventing the leg muscles from aligning along lateral push vectors and giving insufficient ground leverage.
The split step is timed too early or too low, forcing the player to land before visually recognizing where the ball is going.
The player lacks the triple bend at the knee, hip, and ankle, leaving the legs too straight to recruit stabilizing musculature.
The brain subconsciously forces a narrow stance to protect soft tissue because the lower body lacks the conditioning to absorb high landing forces.

angles.summary: Pushing from a wide stance directs force vectors laterally to generate left-and-right movement and reflexive balance adjustments.
Running from a standstill takes three slow steps, whereas landing into motion utilizes stored elastic energy like a continuous sprint.
Achieving an effective athletic base will initially feel comically wide compared to what you are used to.
Federer recovers with narrow feet and heels down when he thinks he missed, but instantly widens and loads when he realizes the ball is in.
Single-leg balance allows a player to selectively delay foot contact and let gravity initiate lateral acceleration toward a volley.

solutions.summary: Split step late enough and jump high enough so you recognize ball direction in the air and land directly in motion.
Perform fast-feet line taps moving one foot back and forth across a court line while the other taps in place moving up and down the court.
Practice simple low hops on one foot focusing purely on a triple-bend landing to absorb force through the hip and thigh.
Perform single-leg lateral jumps, pausing and holding each landing for a full countdown to completely absorb force before jumping back.
Execute the single-leg lateral jumping drill with hands held behind your back so that balance is generated entirely by the lower body.
